Nu misstänks han för flera brott. – Det är ett av de större vapenbeslagen som gjorts i Sverige, säger åklagare Jacob Semark. Mannen greps den 30 december 2025 och har suttit häktad sedan i januari tidigare i år. Det var när civila poliser fattade misstankar om att mannen var narkotikapåverkad och kunde ha narkotika i sin bostad som en husrannsakan genomfördes och vapnen hittades. Flera av dem var fungerande skjutvapen. – Han har sagt att han fått vapnen och föremålen av släktingar, säger Jacob Semark, åklagaren i fallet. Vad säger du om den förklaringen? – Jag kan inte ge någon förklaring på varför han hade vapnen, mer än att det kanske är som han säger, men han får ändå inte ha vapnen. Han har ingen vapenlicens. Mängder av nazistföremål i bostaden På bilder i förundersökningsprotokollet syns även stora mängder nazistföremål i mannens bostad, bland annat en byst av Hitler, flera nazistiska flaggor och nazistuniformer. Det finns även bilder och videor på när han heilar, uttalar nazistiska slagord och poserar med SS-flaggor. – Det har vi givetvis tittat på, men utredningen har inte kunnat ge något svar på syftet, men han säger själv att han är intresserad av andra världskriget, säger Jacob Semark. Är han nazist? – Det kan jag inte säga att man kan belägga, men han har ett intresse för det. Har ni utrett om han är del av något kriminellt nätverk? – Såvitt vi har kunnat, men det verkar inte som att han är det. Mannen själv förnekar att han är nazist och säger i förhör att det handlar om ”en skämtjargong” och satir. Nekar till brott Förutom olika vapen hittades även ett hölje till en bomb, elva pyrotekniska pjäser, tolv tårgasfacklor, signalpatroner och flera stubintrådar. Nu åtalas mannen för synnerligen grovt vapenbrott, brott mot vapenlagen, brott mot lagen om brandfarliga och explosiva varor och ringa narkotikabrott. Han nekar till brott. Kalmar bortaslog Degerfors med 2–1 i det allsvenska ångestmötet och klättrar upp på säker mark i tabellen. – Sjukt skönt. Bara att få göra mål är extra bra för det här laget, säger Vilmer Tyrén till SVT Sport. Efter sju matchers måltorka bröts Kalmars förbannelse direkt på Stora Valla. Gästerna rivstartade och gjorde mål redan i den tredje minuten, efter att hemmalagets Daniel Sundgren slagit bort bollen. – Jag sätter laget i skiten efter bara några minuter. Vi lockar dem till en bra press och i det momentet är vi inte tillräckligt skickliga, dels jag men även lagkamrater, säger Sundgren. Det var Marius Söderbäck som därefter fick läget att göra 1-0 och Vilmer Tyrén kunde snart utöka till 2-0 för Kalmar. Men halvvägs in i halvleken blev det en scenförändring. Degerfors hade två ribbträffar och en boll i stolpen innan Nahom Netabay till slut reducerade strax före pausvilan. Netabay: ”Vi spelade som juniorer” – Vi spelade som juniorer första 20. De fick mycket övertag där i början och sedan försöker vi återhämta oss. Men vi hade behövt 2–2 före paus när vi hade tryck, säger en besviken Nahom Netabay till SVT Sport. Den andra halvleken blev mållös trots att Kalmar hade flera vassa lägen. Degerfors-målvakten Matvei Igonen stod för ett par kvalificerade räddningar och Kalmar hade också ett par frilägen där försvararna i sista stund hann emellan. – Vi är bra framåt och borde ha gjort fler än två mål i dag. Vi fick grymt bra energi i starten, första 25 är grymma, säger Vilmer Tyrén. Säsongens första bortaseger Kalmar var inför matchen seriens sämsta bortalag med bara två poäng på 12 matcher. Det här var deras första bortaseger för säsongen. – Det var mycket som klickade i dag. Det var på tiden men det viktigaste var tre poäng, konstaterar Carl Gustafsson. Lagen byter nu plats i tabellen och Kalmar går upp på säker mark med 22 poäng, två före Degerfors på kvalplats. Nästjumbon Örgryte har 18. – Det är tufft just nu, det tar jättehårt. Årets nomineringar till Augustpriset är här, och listan innehåller allt från ungdomskärlek till tankar om döden och en studie av fiskars inre tankeliv. 18 litterära verk har chans att tilldelas Augustpriset. Idag tillkännagavs årets nominerade i kategorierna Årets svenska skönlitterära bok, Årets fackbok och Årets barn- och ungdomsbok. De sex titlar som nominerats till det Lilla Augustpriset presenterades. – Det här är alltid en jättepirrig dag, säger Mikaela Zabrodsky, VD för Svenska Förläggareföreningen som delar ut Augustpriset. sources.title: Curfew imposed in parts of central Paris and other cities after rioting across France
sources.summary: It comes after the country's interior minister admits that police "lost control" in some cities.
sources.text: Figure caption, Are the riots in France a warning of an intense election to come? By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 19 October 2026 French authorities have imposed overnight curfews in parts of central Paris and other cities after a weekend of riots and looting across the country. Police in Paris said a curfew would be in force between 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) and 06:00 in Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area. A ban on unauthorised gatherings has also been imposed in several other parts of the city centre. Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were announced for cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north. Earlier Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez, who has been strongly criticised by opposition politicians over the preparedness for the disorder but whose resignation was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron, admitted police had "lost control" in some cities. The protests began last month with students demanding better school conditions, but they have since escalated to take in a broader range of concerns, with numbers at demonstrations this weekend bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups. More than 2,500 people have been arrested, officials said. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured. Following a crisis meeting on Monday, the prime minister said local mayors were being given the power to implement curfews "where they need", without specifying which cities where they would be enforced. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu, who did not rule out imposing a state of emergency in the country, said the government would also set aside money to help affected areas recover from the damage, and the funding would be recovered from those behind the violence. "There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay," Lecornu said. He also announced a partial unemployment fund for those who could not work as a result of the riots and looting. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, French police officers stop a vehicle entering the curfew zone in Lyon Meanwhile, NuÃ±ez said 200 investigators were analysing CCTV footage to try to identify possible ringleaders. He attempted to resign on Sunday, but Macron refused "given the need for continued command of law enforcement", the ÃlysÃ©e Palace said. The statement said NuÃ±ez should be transparent over what Macron called "intelligence and foresight failings". More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) says. Its head Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that damage from the riots was estimated at "hundreds of millions of euros". Jean-Luc Chauvin, the president of the CCI's Marseille branch, told the BBC that many of the city's shop owners were in "deep distress" and fear for their survival. Looted goods have been listed on certain selling platforms, two French government ministers said. A Vinted spokesperson said the sale or solicitation of stolen goods was "strictly prohibited". "Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," it said. Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale Published 10 hours ago Figure caption, 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Some 550,000 demonstrators took to the streets over the weekend for protests against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools. Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns. In the central city of Limoges, the ornate 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire started by rioters on Saturday, its clock tower and roof collapsing as the flames took hold. The US Embassy in France has issued an alert advising its citizens to avoid areas affected by the recent demonstrations. The warning says to "exercise caution" if they find themselves close to large gatherings. China and Germany have issued similar warnings. Some politicians have accused the left-wing La France Insoumise party of playing a role in the violence, with Lecornu alleging in an earlier news conference that some groups "want to create chaos in our country up until the presidential elections". The party's leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon, who will stand in next year's presidential election, responded by calling for the French PM to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder". The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside". "This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage. She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget". "Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote. sources.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
sources.summary: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing.
sources.text: Image source, Naomi-Scherbel Ball/BBC Image caption, Serhii Beskrestnov said "people have already died" due to lack of warnings about incoming missile attacks By Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent in Kyiv Published 19 October 2026 Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died." The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing. The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine. Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week , as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows. Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the issues are not a coincidence. On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter." Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause. "We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles." But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue. "This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not." He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack." However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component." Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications. Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h). This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas. Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement. Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine. He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'." Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems. He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step. "We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink." On Monday, when asked about intelligence sharing, Trump said: "We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given us nothing." Figure caption, Watch: Moment Ukrainian soldier lifted to safety by drone Earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing. "I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday. Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system." The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response. A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine. The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country. Russian attacks continued late on Monday, with Ukrainian officials saying at least six people were killed - including a toddler in her pram and an 11-year-old girl - in a drone strike near a park cafÃ© in the north-eastern Kharkiv region. Zelensky described the attack in which another 14 people were injured as "absolute atrocity". sources.title: Kenya cult leader who told parents to starve children guilty of 191 murders
sources.summary: Self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie was found guilty of 191 murder charges - all but one of them children.
sources.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Paul Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", the judge said By Thomas Mukhwana Africa correspondent ,Â Reporting from Shakahola Published 19 October 2026 The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, has been found guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Mackenzie ordered members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus". His doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was "evil". Twenty-eight other leaders of his cult were also convicted of murder. They had all pleaded not guilty, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die. Warning: This article contains details which some people might find distressing. Delivering her eight-hour judgement in the port city of Mombasa, Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece". One of his co-accused said Mackenzie had told his followers that anyone who "resisted the directive to fast must be forced to go to heaven through kicks and blows". Burials inside the forest where the cult was based were called "weddings". Those who died "were celebrated as having wedded with Jesus", the judge said. One witness stated that a pregnant woman had been barred from nursing her new-born baby, who died 12 days later. "She was instructed to fast to death and follow her children," the witness said. Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution. Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult also face a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children. But this is the first time the pastor has faced a verdict on the most serious charges of murder. He is due to be sentenced on 6 November. He was arrested in 2023, after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie had led his followers from across the country. Stephen Mwiti, 48, said he lost all six of his children to the cult. His former wife was one of those convicted of murder alongside Mackenzie. "I'm a happy man, that all persons have been convicted," he told the BBC outside court. "All six of my children died in Shakahola forest," Mwiti said ahead of the verdict, visibly emotional holding a photograph of his family. "I only found and buried the remains of my son Samuel." Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, More than 400 bodies were dug up in Shakahola forest Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (Â£6) a day. "Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old." "We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another." Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets". Although many of Mackenzie's followers were from elsewhere in Kenya, some of the remains are of people who were familiar to the community because the people in the cult would often go to nearby Shakahola town for supplies and to fetch water from the River Galana which flows through the town. "We would sometimes carry people on our motorbikes into the forest," said Salim Karisa, another gravedigger. "But it was so planned and secretive that nobody could tell what was happening inside." Image source, Mohamed Madi / BBC Image caption, Stephen Mwiti said he was happy with the verdict Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in the church's branches across Kenya. His church ran a television station called Times TV which would broadcast his sermons from his church in Malindi. His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil". Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning." The self-proclaimed pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons". Image caption, This is the building from where Mackenzie broadcast his sermons The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him. Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him". When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned. "My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said. The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said. By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers. Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest. He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover. "My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said. "I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest." Image caption, Peter Shukrani says he would have died if he had stayed in the forest but still believes Mackenzie is a good man Many of the bodies are still unidentified owing to their advanced state of decomposition. In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery. Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me". "Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said before the verdict was announced. "I still love him and he is still my pastor." In contrast Dan Mackenzie believed his father should be found guilty of murder. "He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing," also speaking before the verdict. Det skriver han själv på sociala medier. Så här skriver Jimmy Jansson om avhoppet: – Kanske hoppades jag på en nytändning under och efter valet. När den hedervärda frågan om att kandidera till riksdagen kom var det svårt att svara något annat än ja. Jag gjorde det, med reservation för att jag visste att jag behövde få känna efter ordentligt en tid till. Ingen ”nytändning” – Men nytändningen har inte riktigt infunnit sig. Kanske sitter sviterna av många år i politiken kvar? Jag tror att året med över 30 skjutningar satte djupa spår. Jag har aldrig känt samma glädje till politiken igen efter det. Jimmy Jansson säger i sitt inlägg att han fått upp ögonen för ”livet utanför politiken”. Men exakt vad han tänker göra nämner han inte. Han har dock redan flera uppdrag utanför politiken. Bland annat tillträdde han som vd för OK detaljhandel AB för bara några dagar sedan, enligt uppgifter från Bolagsverket. Dessutom driver han eget företag och har flera styrelseuppdrag. Åsa Kullgren, även hon S-politiker från Eskilstuna, tar nu över Jimmy Jansson roll i riksdagen. Det skriver Jansson i sitt inlägg på sociala medier. – Ja, det blir väl så eftersom jag är näst på tur på Sörmlandslistan, säger hon. Åsa Kullgren (S) tar över Hon har känt till att Jimmy Jansson varit på väg att lämna riksdagen. – Vi har haft en dialog om det här och jag har haft information om det ett tag. Hon arbetar vanligtvis som vice chefsåklagare i Örebro, nu blir hon tjänstledig därifrån. På onsdag ska hon infinna sig i riksdagen. – Det var någon på Socialdemokraternas kansli som ringde och berättade det i morse. Hur känns det att nu bli riksdagsledamot? – Det är blandade känslor. Jag trivs bra med mitt jobb och samtidigt ser jag fram emot att tjänstgöra i riksdagen. Åklagaren Åsa Kullgren (S) tar över efter Jimmy Jansson.
